1a.html:
Given: biaxial tensile stress in the xy plane, \sigma_z = 0; e_{xx} = e_{yy} = 0.01; cubic, c_{11} = 3\times10^{11}\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}, c_{12} = 1\times10^{11}\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}, B_1 = 3\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}. The cube axes are taken along x, y, z, with z the film normal, and there are no shear strains.

Find: the magnetoelastic anisotropy.

Solution

Step 1, out-of-plane strain. From the sheet, \sigma_i = c_{11}e_{ii} + c_{12}(e_{jj} + e_{kk}), and the free surface gives \sigma_z = 0:

\begin{aligned} \sigma_z &= c_{11}e_{zz} + c_{12}\left(e_{xx} + e_{yy}\right) = 0 \\ e_{zz} &= -\frac{2c_{12}}{c_{11}}e_{xx} = -\frac{2(1\times10^{11})}{3\times10^{11}}(0.01) = -6.67\times10^{-3} \end{aligned}

The film thins (Poisson contraction) while it is stretched in plane.

Step 2, in-plane stress (for the cross-check):

\sigma_x = c_{11}e_{xx} + c_{12}\left(e_{yy} + e_{zz}\right) = (3\times10^{11})(0.01) + (1\times10^{11})(0.00333) = 3.33\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{Pa}

Step 3, magnetoelastic energy. Straining the lattice changes the crystal field and the overlap of the magnetic orbitals, so the anisotropy energy gains terms linear in strain. With no shear strains the B_2 term is zero. Let \theta be the angle between \mathbf{M} and the film normal, so \alpha_1^2 + \alpha_2^2 = \sin^2\theta and \alpha_3^2 = \cos^2\theta:

\begin{aligned} u_{me} &= B_1\left(\alpha_1^2 e_{xx} + \alpha_2^2 e_{yy} + \alpha_3^2 e_{zz}\right) = B_1\left(e_{xx}\sin^2\theta + e_{zz}\cos^2\theta\right) \\ &= B_1 e_{zz} + B_1\left(e_{xx} - e_{zz}\right)\sin^2\theta \end{aligned}

The in-plane direction of \mathbf{M} does not matter because e_{xx} = e_{yy}: the anisotropy is uniaxial about the normal.

Step 4, the anisotropy constant.

K_{me} = B_1\left(e_{xx} - e_{zz}\right) = B_1 e_{xx}\left(1 + \frac{2c_{12}}{c_{11}}\right) = (3\times10^{6})(0.01 + 0.00667) = 5.0\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}

Step 5, meaning and cross-check. K_{me} > 0 in u = K_{me}\sin^2\theta, so the energy is lowest at \theta = 0: the easy axis is the film normal and the film plane is hard. From the sheet, \lambda_{100} = -\frac{2}{3}B_1/(c_{11} - c_{12}) = -\frac{2}{3}(3\times10^{6})/(2\times10^{11}) = -1.0\times10^{-5}. A material with negative magnetostriction under in-plane tension turns \mathbf{M} away from the tension, and

K_{me} = -\tfrac{3}{2}\lambda_{100}\sigma_x = -\tfrac{3}{2}(-1.0\times10^{-5})(3.33\times10^{9}) = 5.0\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}

Answer: K_{me} = B_1(e_{xx} - e_{zz}) = +5.0\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}, a uniaxial anisotropy with the easy axis normal to the film (perpendicular magnetic anisotropy). The film is actually magnetised perpendicular only if K_{me} beats its shape anisotropy, \mu_0 M_s^2/2, that is for M_s below about 282\ \mathrm{kA\,m^{-1}} (\mu_0 M_s < 0.35 T).
pts: Uses \sigma_z = 0 with \sigma_z = c_{11}e_{zz} + c_{12}(e_{xx} + e_{yy})
e_{zz} = -2c_{12}e_{xx}/c_{11} = -6.67\times10^{-3} (Poisson contraction)
Magnetoelastic energy u_{me} = B_1(\alpha_1^2 e_{xx} + \alpha_2^2 e_{yy} + \alpha_3^2 e_{zz}), B_2 term zero (no shear strain)
Rewrites it as u_{me} = B_1 e_{zz} + B_1(e_{xx} - e_{zz})\sin^2\theta, with \theta from the film normal
K_{me} = B_1(e_{xx} - e_{zz}) = 5.0\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}} with units
Interprets: K_{me} > 0, so the easy axis is the film normal (perpendicular anisotropy) and the plane is hard
Cross-checks with \lambda_{100} = -1.0\times10^{-5} and \sigma = 3.33 GPa, or notes that K_{me} must exceed \mu_0 M_s^2/2 for \mathbf{M} to stand perpendicular
1a.src: Magnetic anisotropy, p 2; Lecture 03 Magnetic ceramics, slide 56; O'Handley, Modern Magnetic Materials, pp 257, 263-265, 293, 669
1a.watch:
• Leaving out the Poisson strain gives B_1 e_{xx} = 3.0\times10^4\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}, 40 % too small. The factor 1 + 2c_{12}/c_{11} = 1.67 is close to 2, which is why thin-film books write K_{me} \approx 2B_1 e.
  • State the sign convention: some texts write the magnetoelastic term as -K\cos^2\theta; either way a positive B_1 under in-plane tension favours the normal.
  • The question gives no B_2, so the film is taken as (001), with its normal along a cube axis. For a (111) film the B_2 (\lambda_{111}) term would set the anisotropy instead.

1b.fix: • Slide 22 of the defects deck gives, at low p_{\mathrm{O_2}}, [\mathrm{O_i^{\prime\prime}}] = K_f(K_v/4)^{1/3}p_{\mathrm{O_2}}^{1/6}. Since [\mathrm{O_i^{\prime\prime}}] = K_f/[\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}] and [\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}] = (K_v/4)^{1/3}p_{\mathrm{O_2}}^{-1/6}, the correct expression is K_f(K_v/4)^{-1/3}p_{\mathrm{O_2}}^{+1/6}. The slope +1/6 is unchanged.
1b.html:
In a Li-ion battery the garnet is the solid electrolyte: it must carry \mathrm{Li^+} but block electrons. I would process and run it in the intermediate, stoichiometric (anti-Frenkel) region, as close as possible to the point where n = p.

Defect equilibria (doubly ionised defects, brackets as site fractions):

\begin{aligned} \mathrm{O_O^{\times}} &\rightleftharpoons \tfrac12\mathrm{O_2(g)} + \mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}} + 2e^{\prime}, & K_v &= [\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}]\,n^2\,p_{\mathrm{O_2}}^{1/2} \\ \tfrac12\mathrm{O_2(g)} &\rightleftharpoons \mathrm{O_i^{\prime\prime}} + 2h^{\bullet}, & K_i &= [\mathrm{O_i^{\prime\prime}}]\,p^2\,p_{\mathrm{O_2}}^{-1/2} \\ \mathrm{O_O^{\times}} &\rightleftharpoons \mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}} + \mathrm{O_i^{\prime\prime}}, & K_F &= [\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}][\mathrm{O_i^{\prime\prime}}] \end{aligned}

Electroneutrality: n + 2[\mathrm{O_i^{\prime\prime}}] = p + 2[\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}].

The three regions

  • Low p_{\mathrm{O_2}}: n = 2[\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}] \propto p_{\mathrm{O_2}}^{-1/6}, an n-type electronic conductor.
  • High p_{\mathrm{O_2}}: p = 2[\mathrm{O_i^{\prime\prime}}] \propto p_{\mathrm{O_2}}^{+1/6}, a p-type conductor.
  • Intermediate: [\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}] = [\mathrm{O_i^{\prime\prime}}] = K_F^{1/2}, independent of p_{\mathrm{O_2}}, while n = K_v^{1/2}K_F^{-1/4}p_{\mathrm{O_2}}^{-1/4} and p = K_i^{1/2}K_F^{-1/4}p_{\mathrm{O_2}}^{+1/4} are both small.

Why the middle region

  1. Electronic conduction self-discharges the cell, and electrons inside the electrolyte reduce \mathrm{Li^+} to Li metal, which grows dendrites and short-circuits it. So the electron-rich low-p_{\mathrm{O_2}} and hole-rich high-p_{\mathrm{O_2}} regions are rejected.
  2. Setting n = p gives p_{\mathrm{O_2}}^{*} = K_v/K_i, the minimum electronic conductivity (equal mobilities). The window runs from K_v^2/16K_F^3 to 16K_F^3/K_i^2. This is the electrolytic domain, where the ionic transference number is close to 1.
  3. The crystal stays stoichiometric, with defects fixed by K_F(T) alone. Its composition and lattice parameter do not drift as the electrode potentials change during cycling.

Design: sinter and anneal near p_{\mathrm{O_2}}^{*}, and choose dopants that widen the window, since the Li anode is strongly reducing and the cathode oxidising.
pts: Identifies the oxide as the solid electrolyte: high \mathrm{Li^+} conduction with negligible electronic conduction
Writes the three defect reactions with their mass-action constants K_v, K_i and K_F, and the electroneutrality condition
Low p_{\mathrm{O_2}}: n = 2[\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}] \propto p_{\mathrm{O_2}}^{-1/6}, n-type, so rejected
High p_{\mathrm{O_2}}: p = 2[\mathrm{O_i^{\prime\prime}}] \propto p_{\mathrm{O_2}}^{+1/6}, p-type, so rejected

Intermediate: [\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}] = [\mathrm{O_i^{\prime\prime}}] = K_F^{1/2} independent of p_{\mathrm{O_2}}; n \propto p_{\mathrm{O_2}}^{-1/4} and p \propto p_{\mathrm{O_2}}^{+1/4} are small
Chooses the middle region near n = p, p_{\mathrm{O_2}}^{*} = K_v/K_i, where electronic conductivity is lowest (or gives the window limits)
Gives the cost of electronic leakage: self-discharge, Li dendrites and short circuit
Notes that stoichiometry is fixed in this region (stable composition), and that processing should be done at this p_{\mathrm{O_2}}

• Axes: log [defect] against log p_{\mathrm{O_2}}, three regions separated by vertical lines.
  • Low p_{\mathrm{O_2}}: n and [\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}] with slope -1/6; high p_{\mathrm{O_2}}: p and [\mathrm{O_i^{\prime\prime}}] with slope +1/6.

1b.watch:
• The oxygen defects of the middle region are not the \mathrm{Li^+} carriers. The region is chosen because it has the lowest electronic conductivity and a fixed composition.
  • The window exists only if K_F is large compared with K_0 = np. If electronic disorder dominates (Fig. 2.12 on slide 24), the middle region has n = p flat and much higher electronic leakage.
  • Convention: brackets are site fractions, and n, p are written for [e^{\prime}], [h^{\bullet}] as on the slides. The 1/16 factors change if you count per formula unit, but the slopes do not.

2a.html:
The structure is a magnetic tunnel junction (MTJ): NiFe is the free (storage) layer, MgO the insulating tunnel barrier, Co the reference layer, and IrMn an antiferromagnet that pins the Co.

Storing the bit.

  • NiFe (permalloy) is magnetically soft. Its in-plane uniaxial anisotropy (induced, plus shape anisotropy if the cell is elongated along the arrow) gives two stable remanent states, along +x or -x.
  • Exchange coupling to IrMn holds the Co magnetization fixed in one direction.
  • The bit is the relative orientation: NiFe parallel to Co (P) = "0", antiparallel (AP) = "1". Both states exist at zero field and are separated by a barrier K_uV \gtrsim 60k_BT, so the memory is non-volatile.

Reading. Pass a small sense current through the connected wires, perpendicular to the layers, and measure the resistance. Electrons cross the MgO by tunnelling without spin flip, and each spin channel's conductance is proportional to the product of that spin's densities of states at E_F in the two electrodes. In P, majority electrons tunnel into majority states and R_P is low. In AP, majority states face minority states and R_{AP} is high. This is tunnelling magnetoresistance, which in Julliere's model is

\mathrm{TMR} = \frac{R_{AP}-R_P}{R_P} = \frac{2P_1P_2}{1-P_1P_2}

with P_1, P_2 the spin polarisations of the two electrodes. Comparing with a reference resistor gives the bit. The sense current is too small to switch NiFe, so reading does not destroy the bit.

Writing. Send a current pulse I along the second wire. Its field, about H = I/2\pi r at distance r, lies along the easy axis at the cell. H must exceed the NiFe switching field but stay well below the field that would unpin Co. The sign of I sets NiFe along +x or -x, writing P or AP. In an array, each cell sits where two current lines cross: either field alone is below the switching field, but together they lie outside the Stoner-Wohlfarth astroid, so only the addressed cell switches. Modern cells may instead use spin-transfer torque: a large current through the stack, whose direction chooses P or AP.
pts: Identifies NiFe as the soft free (storage) layer, Co as the reference layer pinned by IrMn, and MgO as the tunnel barrier
Bit is the relative orientation, NiFe parallel ("0") or antiparallel ("1") to Co along the easy axis; both remanent, so non-volatile
Read: small current through the connected wires, perpendicular to the layers, and the resistance measured against a reference
Explains TMR: spin-conserving tunnelling, conductance set by the spin-resolved densities of states; R_P low, R_{AP} high, \mathrm{TMR} = 2P_1P_2/(1-P_1P_2)
States that readout is non-destructive because the sense current cannot switch NiFe
Write: current pulse in the second wire gives a field H \approx I/2\pi r along the easy axis; the current direction chooses P or AP
Field window: above the NiFe switching field, well below the field that unpins Co
Selects one cell in an array by coincident currents (Stoner-Wohlfarth astroid), or names spin-transfer-torque writing

• Cross-section of the stack, bottom to top: IrMn, Co with a fixed arrow (right), thin MgO, NiFe with an arrow right (P, "0", low R) and a second copy with the NiFe arrow left (AP, "1", high R).
  • Resistance against field along the easy axis: a square loop between R_P and R_{AP}, switching at \pm H_{sw} of NiFe, with Co unchanged over the whole field range.
  • The write wire over the cell with current into the page and circular field lines, the field at NiFe parallel to the easy axis.
2a.src: O'Handley, Modern Magnetic Materials, pp 621-622, 629-635, 740-744; Anisotropy and domain walls, slides 3-6; Single-domain particles and reversal, slides 1-2; Standard textbook treatment
2a.watch:
• The bit is not the absolute direction of either layer; only NiFe switches and the resistance reports its orientation relative to Co.
  • O'Handley writes Julliere's result as \Delta G/G = 2P_1P_2/(1+P_1P_2), normalised to the parallel conductance; it is the same physics as \Delta R/R_P. Define the ratio you quote.
  • With P = 0.35 for Co (O'Handley Table 15.2) on both sides, Julliere gives a TMR of 28%. Amorphous \mathrm{Al_2O_3} barriers give tens of percent; crystalline MgO gives several hundred percent (part b).
  • Scale: I = 1\ \mathrm{mA} at r = 100\ \mathrm{nm} gives only H = 1.6\ \mathrm{kA\,m^{-1}} (\mu_0H = 2\ \mathrm{mT}). Shape anisotropy raises the switching field of a small patterned element to several millitesla, so field-written MRAM needs write currents of several mA; this power cost is one reason spin-transfer torque took over.

2b.html:
Role of the MgO.

  1. It is the insulating tunnel barrier (band gap about 7.8 eV) between the two ferromagnets. Current can cross only by quantum tunnelling, which conserves spin, so the junction resistance depends on whether NiFe and Co are parallel or antiparallel. This tunnelling magnetoresistance is what reads the bit.
  2. It separates the two ferromagnets, so NiFe can switch while Co stays fixed.
  3. Crystalline (001) MgO is also a spin filter: Bloch states of \Delta_1 symmetry decay most slowly through it, and in bcc Fe, Co and CoFe(B) electrodes these states are almost fully spin polarised. The TMR therefore reaches 200 to 600% at room temperature, against tens of percent for amorphous \mathrm{Al_2O_3} barriers.

Thickness: about 1 to 2 nm, only 5 to 10 atomic layers (layer spacing a/2 = 0.21 nm). The tunnelling probability falls exponentially with thickness t:

T \propto \exp(-2\kappa t), \qquad \kappa = \frac{\sqrt{2m\phi}}{\hbar} \approx 5.1\ \mathrm{nm^{-1}}\ \text{for}\ \phi = 1\ \mathrm{eV}

so each extra 0.1 nm multiplies the resistance by about 2.8.

  • Too thin (below about 0.8 nm): pinholes short the junction, it breaks down at low voltage, and NiFe couples to Co (orange-peel and interlayer exchange), so the TMR is lost.
  • Too thick (above about 2 to 3 nm): the resistance becomes very large, so the read current and signal are small and reading is slow.

t is set to give a resistance-area product of about 1 to 100 \Omega\,\mu\mathrm{m^2}, a cell resistance of order kilohms.

Purpose of the IrMn. IrMn (about 5 to 10 nm) is an antiferromagnet. Exchange coupling across the IrMn/Co interface gives the Co a unidirectional (exchange) anisotropy, which shifts the Co hysteresis loop along the field axis by the exchange-bias field

H_{eb} = \frac{J_{int}}{\mu_0 M_s t_{Co}}

(J_{int} = interfacial coupling energy per area, t_{Co} = Co thickness). Co is thus pinned: it does not switch in the write fields that reverse NiFe, so it is a fixed reference for the read. The pinning direction is set by cooling through the IrMn blocking temperature in a field along the easy axis. IrMn has no net moment, so it adds no stray field and ignores applied fields.
pts: MgO is the insulating tunnel barrier; spin-conserving tunnelling makes the resistance depend on the relative orientation (TMR), which reads the bit
MgO separates and decouples NiFe and Co so that they switch independently
Crystalline (001) MgO filters \Delta_1 states, giving TMR of hundreds of percent against tens of percent for amorphous \mathrm{Al_2O_3}
Thickness about 1 to 2 nm, because transmission falls as \exp(-2\kappa t) with \kappa \approx 5\ \mathrm{nm^{-1}}
Too thin gives pinholes, breakdown and interlayer coupling; too thick gives a high resistance-area product and a weak, slow read
IrMn is an antiferromagnet that pins Co by interfacial exchange coupling (exchange bias), shifting the Co loop by H_{eb}
Pinned Co is the fixed reference so only NiFe switches when writing; the direction is set by field cooling through the blocking temperature
IrMn has no net moment: no stray field on the free layer and no response to applied fields
2b.sketch:
• Energy diagram across the stack: two metal electrodes with a rectangular MgO barrier of height \phi and width t; a wavefunction decaying exponentially inside the barrier.
  • M-H loop of the stack along the easy axis: a narrow NiFe loop centred near H = 0 and a Co loop shifted to -H_{eb}, with the P and AP plateaus labelled.
2b.src: O'Handley, Modern Magnetic Materials, pp 464-466, 629-635, 739-740; Standard textbook treatment
2b.watch:
• "Thickness" wants a number with a reason: a few nanometres or less, set by the exponential dependence of tunnelling on t. Answers of 10 nm or more are wrong for a tunnel barrier.
  • The spin-filter effect needs crystalline MgO with (001) texture on bcc electrodes (in practice CoFeB, crystallised by annealing at about 300 to 400 degrees C). The NiFe and Co of the sketch are the textbook version.
  • The exchange-bias field is inversely proportional to the Co thickness, so the pinned layer is kept thin, a few nanometres.
  • Extra depth: practical stacks pin the reference with a synthetic antiferromagnet (Co/Ru/Co) on top of IrMn to cancel the reference layer's own stray field on the free layer.

2c.html:
On balance a bad idea, although it could work. A hard magnet (for example CoPt) with coercivity far above the write field could serve as the reference, as in early pseudo-spin-valve MRAM. But:

  1. Stray field. Its large net moment puts a dipolar field on the NiFe, offsetting its loop, so writing "0" and "1" needs unequal fields; it also disturbs neighbouring cells.
  2. Unreliable reference. Its switching fields are spread and it can decay thermally, so repeated write pulses may partly reverse it.

IrMn has no net moment, no stray field and a fixed bias direction, so it pins better.
pts: Gives a verdict with its reason: a high-coercivity reference works in principle (pseudo-spin valve) but is worse than IrMn
The hard magnet's net moment gives a stray field on NiFe: offset loop, unequal write fields, disturbance of neighbours
The hard layer can itself be partly switched (switching-field distribution, thermal decay) by write or stray fields, losing the reference
Contrasts IrMn: zero net moment, no stray field, insensitive to applied fields, fixed unidirectional bias
2c.src: O'Handley, Modern Magnetic Materials, pp 464-465, 742-744; Single-domain particles and reversal, slides 1-2; Standard textbook treatment
2c.watch:
• Either verdict can score if it is argued; the marks are for the stray-field and stability arguments, not the word "good" or "bad".
  • The Co reference layer itself also has a stray field; practical cells cancel it with a synthetic antiferromagnet (Co/Ru/Co) pinned by IrMn.

3a.html:
Given: barium ferrite particles, K_u = 5\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}; printed k = 1.38\times10^{-23}\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}.

Find: the smallest particle diameter that still holds a recorded bit, and the assumptions behind it.

Solution. Below a critical volume, thermal energy flips the particle's moment (superparamagnetism) and the tape forgets the data.

Step 1, criterion. A single-domain uniaxial particle must cross an energy barrier K_uV to reverse. The switching probability per second is

P = \nu_0\exp\left(-\frac{K_uV}{k_BT}\right), \qquad \nu_0 \approx 10^{9}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}

Require that fewer than 10% of the particles flip during the storage time t, so Pt \le 0.1:

\frac{K_uV}{k_BT} \ge \ln(10\,\nu_0\,t)

Step 2, numbers. Archival tape: t = 10 years = 3.16\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{s}, at T = 300\ \mathrm{K}:

\begin{aligned} \ln(10 \times 10^{9} \times 3.16\times10^{8}) &= 42.6 \\ k_BT &= (1.38\times10^{-23}\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}})(300\ \mathrm{K}) = 4.14\times10^{-21}\ \mathrm{J} \\ V_{\min} &= \frac{42.6 \times 4.14\times10^{-21}\ \mathrm{J}}{5\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}} = 3.53\times10^{-26}\ \mathrm{m^3} \\ d_{\min} &= \left(\frac{6V_{\min}}{\pi}\right)^{1/3} = \left(6.74\times10^{-26}\ \mathrm{m^3}\right)^{1/3} = 4.07\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}

With the slides' rule K_uV = 25k_BT (stable for only about a second), V = 2.07\times10^{-26}\ \mathrm{m^3} and d = 3.4 nm.

Answer: d_{\min} \approx 4 nm (4.1 nm for 10-year storage at 300 K; 3.4 nm with the 25k_BT rule). Because d \propto (\ln t)^{1/3}, even 1000 years needs only 4.2 nm.

Assumptions

  1. Each particle is a single domain, uniformly magnetised, and reverses by coherent rotation (Stoner-Wohlfarth), so the barrier is K_uV.
  2. Only the uniaxial magnetocrystalline anisotropy counts; shape anisotropy and the temperature dependence of K_u are ignored.
  3. The particles do not interact and sit in zero field. Stray fields from neighbours or the head would lower the barrier to K_uV(1 - H/H_K)^2.
  4. All particles are spheres of one size (V = \pi d^3/6), with no spread in size or anisotropy.
  5. Thermal activation follows the Arrhenius form with \nu_0 \approx 10^{9}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}, at room temperature (300 K), for the stated storage time.
  6. The particles stay below the critical single-domain size, which sets the upper limit.
pts: Identifies the limit as superparamagnetism: thermal flipping over the barrier K_uV erases the data
Writes P = \nu_0\exp(-K_uV/k_BT), or \tau = \tau_0\exp(K_uV/k_BT), with \nu_0 \approx 10^{9}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}
Sets a criterion tied to a storage time: K_uV \ge 25k_BT (seconds) or about 40 to 43 k_BT (years)
k_BT = 4.14\times10^{-21} J at 300 K and V_{\min} = 3.5\times10^{-26}\ \mathrm{m^3} (or 2.1\times10^{-26}\ \mathrm{m^3} with 25k_BT)
Converts the volume to a diameter with V = \pi d^3/6
Final d_{\min} \approx 4 nm (4.1 nm for 10 years, or 3.4 nm with 25k_BT), with units
Assumptions: single domain, coherent rotation, barrier from the uniaxial crystal anisotropy alone (no shape term), K_u constant at 300 K
Assumptions: identical, non-interacting spheres in zero field, with stated \nu_0, temperature and storage time
3a.src: Single-domain particles and reversal, slides 5-6, 9, 14; Anisotropy and domain walls, slide 8; O'Handley, Modern Magnetic Materials, pp 333-334, 720
3a.watch:
• The question asks for a diameter: do not stop at the volume or the radius (r = 2.0 nm).
  • State the storage time you assume. The slides' 25k_BT rule only guarantees about a second; data tape must last years, so about 40k_BT is the honest criterion. Slide 6 of the single-domain deck gives the same result in its one-year form, r = (10k_BT/K_u)^{1/3} = 2.0 nm.
  • Real \mathrm{BaFe_{12}O_{19}} has K_u \approx 3.2\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}} (O'Handley), which would give d_{\min} \approx 10 nm for 10 years. Use the printed value in the exam.
  • A real tape has a size distribution. The smallest particles must meet the criterion, so the mean size is made larger, and designers use about 60k_BT to allow for interaction fields.

3b.fix: • Slide 7 of the single-domain deck (right-hand figure) draws the coercivity in the superparamagnetic range (D < D_s) as a flat line above the axis. The coercivity there is zero, as slide 5 of the same deck states ("no remanence, no coercivity") and as the left-hand figure on slide 7 draws. Draw H_c = 0 up to D_s.
3b.html:
Coercivity is zero for the smallest particles, rises steeply, peaks in the stable single-domain range (near the critical single-domain size D_c on the slides' sketch) and then falls, first by incoherent reversal and then, above D_c, by wall motion as the particles become multidomain.

Regimes, from small to large diameter D:

  1. Superparamagnetic, D < D_s (K_uV < 25k_BT). Thermal energy reverses each moment within the measurement time, so H_c = 0 and M_r = 0. The assembly behaves as a paramagnet of giant moments M_sV.
  2. Thermally assisted single domain, just above D_s. Thermal activation helps the field over the barrier:
H_c = \frac{2K_u}{\mu_0M_s}\left[1 - 5\left(\frac{k_BT}{K_uV}\right)^{1/2}\right] = H_K\left[1-\left(\frac{D_s}{D}\right)^{3/2}\right]

so H_c climbs steeply with D.

  1. Stable single domain, coherent rotation. No thermal flipping and no domain wall, so H_c approaches the Stoner-Wohlfarth value, H_K = 2K_u/\mu_0M_s for aligned particles (about 0.48H_K for random ones). This is the maximum.
  2. Larger single-domain particles. Curling, buckling or fanning reverse the particle at lower fields, and H_c falls roughly as 1/D^2.
  3. Multidomain, D > D_c. Wall energy (proportional to D^2) is now cheaper than the stray-field energy saved (proportional to D^3), so walls form. Wall motion reverses the particle easily, and H_c falls roughly as 1/D towards the bulk value.

Scale: D_s \approx 12 nm for K_u = 10^{5}\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}} (one-second criterion, r \approx 6 nm); D_c is tens of nanometres (about 50 nm for Fe).

M-H loops

  • Superparamagnetic: no hysteresis. An S-shaped (Langevin) curve passes through the origin, M = N\mu L(\mu_0\mu H/k_BT) with \mu = M_sV, so H_c = 0 and M_r = 0.
  • Single domain, easy axis along H: a square loop with M_r = M_s and H_c = H_K. A random assembly gives M_r = 0.5M_s and H_c \approx 0.48H_K; along the hard axis the curve is linear and reversible.
  • Multidomain: a narrow, sheared loop with low H_c and M_r and a steep initial rise from wall motion.

3c.html:
The Stoner-Wohlfarth model assumes a perfect, uniformly magnetised particle that reverses by coherent rotation at 0 K. It therefore gives the upper limit, H_{sw} \le H_K = 2K_u/\mu_0M_s. Real particles switch at lower fields because:

  1. Incoherent reversal. Above a few exchange lengths, curling, buckling or fanning reverse the moment with less stray-field energy, hence at a lower field.
  2. Nucleation at defects. Surfaces, corners, oxide shells and regions of low anisotropy nucleate a small reversed region that then spreads.
  3. Thermal activation over the barrier in a finite time: H_c = H_K[1 - 5(k_BT/K_uV)^{1/2}].
  4. Interactions and misalignment. Neighbours' stray fields add to the applied field, and tilted easy axes switch earlier (H_K/2 at 45 degrees).
pts: SW assumes coherent rotation of a uniform, defect-free particle with no thermal energy, so H_K = 2K_u/\mu_0M_s is an upper limit
Incoherent modes (curling, buckling, fanning) in particles larger than the coherence size switch at lower fields
Reversal nucleates at defects, surfaces or low-anisotropy regions and spreads
Thermal activation in a finite measuring time lowers H_c, H_c = H_K[1 - 5(k_BT/K_uV)^{1/2}]
Interparticle stray fields or misaligned easy axes lower the switching field
3c.src: Single-domain particles and reversal, slides 1-3, 8, 14; O'Handley, Modern Magnetic Materials, pp 347-351
3c.watch:
• The gap between the measured coercivity and H_K in real magnets is called Brown's coercivity paradox; it is usually explained by nucleation at defects.
  • Misalignment alone does not explain it fully: a single particle's switching field never drops below H_K/2 (the 45 degree point on the astroid).

4a.html:
Why single-phase zirconia is not tough. Toughening needs a phase that can transform under stress. A single-phase zirconia has none:

  • Pure \mathrm{ZrO_2} (monoclinic at room temperature). It is tetragonal at the sintering temperature and turns monoclinic on cooling (near 950^\circ\mathrm{C}) by a martensitic shear with about 4 to 5% volume expansion (slide 13 lattice parameters: 134.2 to 140.6\ \text{\AA}^3). The expansion cracks the part, and at room temperature everything has already transformed.
  • Fully stabilised cubic zirconia (about 8 mol% \mathrm{Y_2O_3} or more). Cubic is kept down to room temperature, so nothing transforms at a crack tip and K_{IC} is only about 3\ \mathrm{MPa\,m^{1/2}}, like other oxides.

Design (phase diagram). Add less stabiliser than full stabilisation needs, so that a metastable tetragonal phase is retained:

  1. Composition in the t + c field: 3 to 8 mol% \mathrm{Y_2O_3} (slide 15), for example 5 mol%.
  2. Solution treat in the cubic field (about 1950^\circ\mathrm{C} at 5 mol%), then cool fast.
  3. Age in the t + c field (about 1400^\circ\mathrm{C}): fine, coherent t lenses (about 40%) grow in the cubic grains.
  4. Stop below the critical size (about 0.2\ \mu\mathrm{m}) and cool. Below the eutectoid (about 560^\circ\mathrm{C}) equilibrium is m + c, but the constrained t precipitates survive.

Alternatives: TZP (2 to 3 mol% \mathrm{Y_2O_3}, all-t grains below about 0.5\ \mu\mathrm{m}) and zirconia-toughened alumina (10 to 20 vol% fine t-\mathrm{ZrO_2} held by the alumina matrix).

Why it works. The crack-tip stress triggers t to m in a zone of half-width w. The expansion, constrained by the matrix, compresses the crack tip and faces (shielding):

K_{tip} = K_{applied} - \Delta K_T, \qquad \Delta K_T \propto V_t\,\varepsilon^{T} E\,\sqrt{w}

K_{IC} rises from about 3 to 6 to 15\ \mathrm{MPa\,m^{1/2}} (Mg-PSZ up to about 20), and strength rises too.
pts: Pure zirconia: t to m on cooling (near 950^\circ\mathrm{C}) with a few percent expansion (4 to 5%; 3 to 5% accepted) cracks the part; at room temperature nothing is left to transform
Fully stabilised cubic zirconia: no transformation possible, K_{IC} about 3\ \mathrm{MPa\,m^{1/2}}

PSZ route: 3 to 8 mol% \mathrm{Y_2O_3}, solution treat in c, cool fast, age in t + c to precipitate fine t
Controls precipitate (or grain) size below the critical size; names TZP or ZTA as alternatives
Mechanism: stress-induced t to m in a zone; constrained expansion compresses the crack, \Delta K_T \propto V_t\,\varepsilon^{T} E\sqrt{w}

4b.html:
Given: \mathrm{Gd_3Ga_5O_{12}} (GGG) substrate, (110), a_s = 12.376 Å; the printed lattice parameters and \lambda_{100}, \lambda_{111} of the rare-earth iron garnets \mathrm{RE_3Fe_5O_{12}}; from the equation sheet, \lambda_{110} = \tfrac{1}{4}\lambda_{100} + \tfrac{3}{4}\lambda_{111}. Not printed, so assumed: garnet E \approx 200 GPa, \nu \approx 0.29.

Find: the garnet film most likely to be magnetised out of plane.

Solution

Step 1, strain from the misfit. A thin coherent film takes the substrate's in-plane spacing, so it carries a biaxial strain and stress

\varepsilon = \frac{a_s - a_f}{a_f}, \qquad \sigma = \frac{E}{1 - \nu}\,\varepsilon \approx 2.8\times10^{11}\,\varepsilon\ \mathrm{Pa}

A film with a larger cell than the substrate (a_f > a_s) is compressed (\varepsilon < 0); a smaller one is in tension.

Step 2, magnetoelastic anisotropy of a (110) film. The film normal is [110], so the magnetostriction that counts is \lambda_{110}. With E = K_{me}\sin^2\theta, \theta measured from the normal (K_{me} > 0 means the normal is easy):

K_{me} = -\tfrac{3}{2}\lambda_{110}\,\sigma

Out-of-plane anisotropy needs \lambda_{110}\varepsilon < 0: compression with \lambda_{110} > 0, or tension with \lambda_{110} < 0.

Step 3, screen the table (\lambda in 10^{-6}):

REa_f (Å)\varepsilon (%)\lambda_{110}K_{me} (\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}})Out of plane?
Y12.3760−2.360no strain
Sm12.530−1.23−1.13-5.8\times10^{3}no
Eu12.498−0.98+6.60+2.7\times10^{4}yes
Gd12.470−0.75−2.13-6.8\times10^{3}no
Tb12.436−0.48+8.18+1.7\times10^{4}yes
Dy12.405−0.23−7.55-7.5\times10^{3}no
Ho12.375+0.01−3.55+1\times10^{2}negligible
Er, Tm, Yb12.349 to 12.302+0.22 to +0.60−3.2, −3.6, −3.0+2.9 to +7.7\times10^{3}weak

Step 4, the two candidates in the (110) plane. A (110) film is not isotropic in its own plane, and \lambda_{110} gives the average. The energy steps from the normal to the two in-plane axes are

K_{[1\bar{1}0]} = -\tfrac{3}{2}\lambda_{111}\,\sigma, \qquad K_{[001]} = -\tfrac{3}{4}\left(\lambda_{100} + \lambda_{111}\right)\sigma

TbIG (\sigma = -1.36 GPa): 2.45\times10^{4} and 8.9\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}. EuIG (\sigma = -2.75 GPa): 7.4\times10^{3} and 4.7\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}. All are positive, but the small \lambda_{111} of EuIG (+1.8) leaves a weak step towards [1\bar{1}0], comparable to the shape anisotropy of a garnet with a YIG-like moment (\mu_0 M_s^2/2 \approx 1.2\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}).

Step 5, choose. TbIG has the largest positive \lambda_{110} (from \lambda_{111} = +12) and half the misfit of EuIG (0.48 % against 0.98 %), so it stays coherently strained to a greater thickness. Its compensation point lies near 250 K, so at 300 K its M_s and shape anisotropy are small.

Answer: grow a thin, coherently strained \mathrm{Tb_3Fe_5O_{12}} film on GGG (110): 0.48 % compression, \lambda_{110} = +8.2\times10^{-6}, K_{me} \approx +1.7\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}, with both in-plane axes higher in energy, so the easy axis is the film normal. EuIG gives the larger average K_{me} (2.7\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}) and is the runner-up; a (Tb,Eu) garnet can tune between them.

Screens the table with correct misfits and \lambda_{110}, for example Eu -0.98 % and +6.6, Tb -0.48 % and +8.2, Dy -0.23 % and -7.55

• The elastic constants are not printed, so the K_{me} values are estimates; the sign rule and the ranking do not depend on them.
  • The printed substrate value, 12.376 Å, is the YIG entry; GGG is usually quoted as 12.383 Å. With it, Tb (-0.43 %) and Eu (-0.92 %) are still compressed and the choice stands.
  • Do not use \lambda_{100} or \lambda_{111} alone for a (110) film; that is the purpose of the printed \lambda_{110}.
  • TbIG's moment at 300 K is several times smaller than YIG's because of its compensation point, which is why its shape anisotropy is a small fraction of 1.2\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}.

5a.html:
The mode is set by the balance of three energies at the edge of a film nucleus, Young's equation (slide 15):

\gamma_s = \gamma_i + \gamma_f\cos\theta

\gamma_s = substrate surface energy, \gamma_f = film surface energy, \gamma_i = film-substrate interface energy, which rises with the lattice misfit; \theta = contact angle.

Frank-van der MerweVolmer-WeberStranski-Krastanov
Growthlayer by layer (2D)islands (3D)layers, then islands
Energy condition\gamma_s \geq \gamma_i + \gamma_f, \theta = 0: film wets\gamma_s < \gamma_i + \gamma_f, \theta > 0: no wettingfirst \gamma_s > \gamma_{io} + \gamma_{fo}, finally \gamma_s < \gamma_i + \gamma_f
Bondingfilm atoms bound more strongly to the substrate than to each otherfilm atoms bound more strongly to each otherstrong at first, weakened by strain
Misfitsmall (lattice-matched), low \gamma_ilarge or incoherent, high \gamma_imoderate, a few percent
Kineticsfast surface diffusionslow surface diffusionenough mobility to form islands
ExamplesSi on Si, TiN on MgO, GaAs on AlAsmetals on \mathrm{SiO_2}, Ag or Au on NaClGe on Si (4% misfit), InP on GaAs, Ag or In on Si

Why each condition works.

  • FvM: covering the substrate removes more energy (\gamma_s) than the new surface and interface cost, so each layer spreads flat and is completed before the next. The film is pseudomorphic.
  • VW: the film lowers its energy by exposing as little interface as possible, so stable clusters grow in three dimensions on the bare substrate.
  • SK: the first pseudomorphic layers wet (\gamma_{io}, \gamma_{fo} for the strained layer). Their coherency strain energy, E_\varepsilon = Y\varepsilon^2 h, rises with every layer, which raises the effective interface energy. After a few monolayers islands, which relax the strain at their free sides, become cheaper than further flat layers.

Kinetics. Low T_{\mathrm{sub}} or a high deposition rate can roughen even a wetting system, because adatoms are buried before they spread.
pts: Young's equation \gamma_s = \gamma_i + \gamma_f\cos\theta, with the three energies and \theta defined, and \gamma_i rising with misfit

FvM needs small misfit and fast diffusion, with an example (Si on Si, TiN on MgO, GaAs on AlAs)
VW: \gamma_s < \gamma_i + \gamma_f, \theta > 0; film atoms bound more strongly to each other; 3D islands
VW example (metals on \mathrm{SiO_2}, Ag or Au on NaCl) and high \gamma_i from a large or incoherent misfit
SK: first layers wet (\gamma_s > \gamma_{io} + \gamma_{fo}), then strain energy Y\varepsilon^2 h grows with thickness until islands are favoured
SK needs a moderate misfit of a few percent, with an example (Ge on Si, InP on GaAs)
Labelled sketch of the three modes
Kinetic remark: low T_{\mathrm{sub}} or high rate roughens growth regardless of the energies

5a.watch:
• Write the inequality the right way round: wetting (FvM) needs \gamma_s larger than \gamma_i + \gamma_f.
  • Slide 3 of the second epitaxy deck notes that Young's equation strictly holds only for liquids; use it as an energy argument for solids.
  • In SK growth the island trigger is strain, not a change in the bulk bond strengths; the islands sit on a wetting layer, unlike VW islands on bare substrate.
  • A large misfit does not always mean islands: with strong bonding the film can stay flat and relax by misfit dislocations above the critical thickness.

5b.html:
Mechanism (slide 20). A higher substrate temperature raises adatom surface mobility, so an adatom can reach the lowest-energy site nearby (a ledge or kink that continues the substrate lattice). Too fast a deposition buries it under later arrivals before it gets there.

Diffusion distance. An adatom wanders for the time between arrivals at a site, \tau_{ad} = N_0/F_{\mathrm{dep}}, so

\delta_{ad} \approx \sqrt{D_{SD}\tau_{ad}} = \left(\frac{N_0 D_0}{F_{\mathrm{dep}}}\right)^{1/2}\exp\left(-\frac{\Delta g^*_{SD}}{2kT_{\mathrm{sub}}}\right)

T_{\mathrm{sub}} up raises \delta_{ad} exponentially; F_{\mathrm{dep}} up lowers it as F_{\mathrm{dep}}^{-1/2}.

Film structure. \delta_{ad} > \delta^*_{\mathrm{epi}}: epitaxial; \delta^*_{\mathrm{poly}} < \delta_{ad} < \delta^*_{\mathrm{epi}}: polycrystalline; \delta_{ad} < \delta^*_{\mathrm{poly}}: amorphous (low T, high flux; slide 75). Setting \delta_{ad} = \delta^*_{\mathrm{epi}} gives the limit

\ln F_{\mathrm{dep}} = -\frac{\Delta g^*_{SD}}{kT_{\mathrm{sub}}} + \ln\frac{N_0 D_0}{(\delta^*_{\mathrm{epi}})^2}

a straight line on \ln(\text{rate}) against 1/T_{\mathrm{sub}}: epitaxy below it (hot, slow), polycrystal above. For Si CVD (slide 20), from the figure, the highest epitaxial rate is about 100 μm/min at 1200 °C but only about 10 μm/min at 1100 °C.

Upper temperature limit. Very hot, growth becomes desorption-limited: \delta_{de} \propto \exp[(\Delta g^*_d - \Delta g^*_{SD})/2kT_{\mathrm{sub}}] falls as T_{\mathrm{sub}} rises, and atoms re-evaporate. A higher flux moves the peak of \delta to a higher temperature.

Conclusion. Epitaxy needs a high T_{\mathrm{sub}} and a low deposition rate; a faster rate demands a hotter substrate.
pts: Mechanism: higher T_{\mathrm{sub}} raises adatom mobility so atoms reach lattice-continuing sites; fast deposition buries them first
\delta_{ad} = (N_0 D_{SD}/F_{\mathrm{dep}})^{1/2} with Arrhenius D_{SD}: rises with T_{\mathrm{sub}}, falls with F_{\mathrm{dep}}
Criterion: \delta_{ad} > \delta^*_{\mathrm{epi}} epitaxial, then polycrystalline, then amorphous below \delta^*_{\mathrm{poly}}
Boundary \ln F_{\mathrm{dep}} = -\Delta g^*_{SD}/kT_{\mathrm{sub}} + \text{const}: epitaxy at high T and low rate, polycrystal above the line
Si CVD example with numbers read from the figure (about 100 μm/min at 1200 °C, 10 at 1100 °C)

5c.fix: • Slide 48 of the 405 evaporation deck prints F_{\mathrm{dep},L} = N_e\cos^n\theta_i\cos\theta_k/(2\pi r^2), without the factor (n+1). That is right only for n = 0; for the cosine source (n = 1) it gives half of the N_e/(\pi r^2) that slides 52-53 of the thin-film deck use. The normalised form is (n+1)N_e\cos^n\theta_i\cos\theta_k/(2\pi r^2) (Ohring p 132), because the emitted flux must add up to N_e over the hemisphere. Thickness ratios d/d_0 are not affected.
5c.html:
Evaporated atoms travel by line of sight, so the flux in any direction is the flux the source emits in that direction (slide 47). With \theta measured from the source normal,

\frac{dN}{d\Omega} = \frac{(n+1)N_e}{2\pi}\cos^n\theta

where N_e is the number of atoms evaporated per second.

  1. Point source, isotropic emission (n = 0). A very small source (wire coil, filament tip) emits equally in all directions, N_e/2\pi per steradian: equal arrows, a hemispherical envelope. The surface of constant flux is a hemisphere of radius H, so F_{\mathrm{dep}} = N_e/(2\pi H^2).
  2. Small planar source, ideal cosine emission (n = 1). A flat melt in a boat or wide crucible, or a Knudsen cell, emits most along the normal and nothing along its own surface: (N_e/\pi)\cos\theta. The envelope is a sphere touching the source; the constant-flux surface is a sphere of diameter H, so F_{\mathrm{dep}} = N_e/(\pi H^2), twice the point value.
  3. Non-ideal, anisotropic small planar source (n > 1). A deep, narrow crucible, with the melt well below its rim, collimates the vapour into a narrow forward lobe; n grows with melt depth over melt area.

On a flat substrate the thickness falls off as d/d_0 = [1 + (L/H)^2]^{-(n+3)/2}: exponent -3/2 for the point source and -2 for the small planar source.

(c) Non-ideal source sketched: narrow forward lobe, n > 1, from a deep, narrow crucible

• The point-source envelope is a hemisphere with all arrows equal; do not draw it as a circle touching the source, which is the cosine source.

6a.html:
Advanced ceramics must meet tight property limits, so composition and microstructure must be controlled from the start. The powder sets the packing of the green body, which sets sintering and the microstructure, which sets the properties (slides 14, 18).

CharacteristicDesiredInterpretation
Particle sizefine, below about 1\ \mu\mathrm{m}large surface energy and short diffusion paths: sintering time scales as d^3 to d^4, so full density at lower temperature, fine grains

6b.fix: The printed question names \mathrm{LaTiO_3} as the pyroelectric. \mathrm{LaTiO_3} is a centrosymmetric orthorhombic perovskite (a \mathrm{Ti^{3+}} Mott insulator), so it cannot be pyroelectric. The pyroelectric on 435-diel slide 9, and the pyroelectric ceramic in Carter, is \mathrm{LiTaO_3} (lithium tantalate); the answer is written for it. 6b.html:
The materials. \mathrm{SiO_2} here means crystalline \alpha-quartz: no centre of symmetry (class 32), so piezoelectric, but no polar axis, so not pyroelectric. The pyroelectric is taken as \mathrm{LiTaO_3}, lithium tantalate (slide 9); \mathrm{LaTiO_3} is centrosymmetric.

Piezoelectric quartz. Stress gives charge (direct effect) and a field gives strain (converse effect):

D = dT + \varepsilon E, \qquad S = dE, \qquad d \approx 2.3\ \mathrm{pC\,N^{-1}}

Its d is small, but quartz has very low loss and a temperature-stable resonance.

  1. Crystal oscillators and filters. An AC voltage makes a thin plate vibrate and the vibration returns charge, so the circuit locks to the resonance, f = v/2t: the clock of watches, computers, phones and radios (stable to about 1 part in 10^{9}).
  2. Pressure and force sensors. A force gives a charge Q = dF; a quartz microbalance also reads deposited film thickness from its resonance shift.

Pyroelectric \mathrm{LiTaO_3}. It is polar and ferroelectric (\theta_c \approx 617^\circ\mathrm{C}). Its spontaneous polarisation falls as it warms, so a change in temperature drives a current:

i = pA\frac{dT}{dt}, \qquad p = \frac{dP_s}{dT} \approx 230\ \mu\mathrm{C\,m^{-2}\,K^{-1}}
  1. Infrared detectors. IR absorbed on a thin blackened slab gives a signal for changes below 10^{-3} K: passive infrared intruder alarms, automatic lights, flame detectors, IR gas analysers.
  2. Thermal imaging and radiometry. Detector arrays in night-vision and fire-fighting cameras; laser power meters.

Pyroelectric (\mathrm{LiTaO_3}) application 2: thermal imaging camera, laser power meter or other radiometer

6c.html:
The dielectric constant is \varepsilon_r = 1 + \chi_e + \chi_i + \chi_d + \chi_s, so it changes whenever one of the four polarisation mechanisms starts or stops working.

Effect of frequency. In an AC field each mechanism contributes only while its charges can keep up with the field reversals. As frequency rises, \varepsilon_r' falls in steps:

  • space charge (interfacial) drops out first, above about 10^{2} to 10^{3} Hz;
  • dipolar (orientation) relaxes at about 10^{7} to 10^{9} Hz;
  • ionic is lost at the infrared resonance, about 10^{13} Hz;
  • electronic is lost at the ultraviolet resonance, about 10^{15} Hz.

At optical frequencies \varepsilon_r = n^2; water falls from 80 to 1.77. The loss \varepsilon'' peaks at each step.

Effect of temperature. It depends on the mechanism:

  • Electronic and ionic polarisation hardly change with T; only thermal expansion alters the ion density and bond stiffness a little. Hence \mathrm{Al_2O_3} and MgO are nearly flat.
  • Dipolar: thermal agitation randomises permanent dipoles, \alpha_d = \mu^2/3kT, so \varepsilon_r falls as 1/T. In a solid the dipoles may be frozen at low T; \varepsilon_r then jumps when they become free (melting or an order-disorder change).
  • Space charge: ion mobility is thermally activated, so at high T the low-frequency \varepsilon_r and the loss rise steeply.
  • Ferroelectrics: \varepsilon_r peaks at each phase change and is highest at the Curie point (\mathrm{BaTiO_3}, 120 °C, about 10^{4}). Above it, \varepsilon_r falls by the Curie-Weiss law, \varepsilon_r = C/(T - T_0).

So \varepsilon_r is highest at low frequency, and at a given frequency it changes with temperature most in polar and ferroelectric materials.
pts: States that \varepsilon_r = 1 + \sum\chi and that each mechanism drops out above its own limiting frequency, so \varepsilon_r' falls stepwise with frequency
Gives the order and ranges: space charge about 10^{2} to 10^{3} Hz, dipolar about 10^{9} Hz, ionic about 10^{13} Hz, electronic about 10^{15} Hz, with \varepsilon_r = n^2 at optical frequencies
Notes that the loss \varepsilon'' peaks at each relaxation or resonance
Electronic and ionic polarisation are nearly independent of temperature
Dipolar: \alpha_d = \mu^2/3kT, so \varepsilon_r falls with rising T; frozen dipoles in a solid make \varepsilon_r jump when they become free
Space charge: thermally activated mobility, so the low-frequency \varepsilon_r and loss rise at high temperature
Ferroelectric: peak at the Curie point (\mathrm{BaTiO_3} 120 °C, about 10^{4}) and Curie-Weiss \varepsilon_r = C/(T - T_0) above it
Sketches \varepsilon_r against log frequency and against temperature

  • Curie-Weiss for \mathrm{BaTiO_3}: C \approx 1.2\times10^{5} K, and T_0 lies about 10 K below \theta_c because the transition is first order.

7a.html:
Parameters. In a ceramic the dielectric constant has two parts (435-bto):

\varepsilon_r = \varepsilon_{r,\mathrm{vol}} + \varepsilon_{r,\mathrm{dom}}

a lattice part from the shift of \mathrm{Ti^{4+}} in its octahedron, and a part from 90° domain walls moving in the field (about 1000 + 700 in a coarse ceramic). Whatever changes either part changes \kappa:

  1. Temperature (crystal structure). \kappa peaks at each phase change (−90 and 5 °C) and is highest, about 10^{4}, at \theta_c = 120^\circ\mathrm{C}; above it \varepsilon_r = C/(T - T_0) with C \approx 1.2\times10^{5} K.
  2. Composition. Shifters in solid solution move \theta_c: \mathrm{Sr^{2+}}, \mathrm{Zr^{4+}}, \mathrm{Sn^{4+}} lower it towards room temperature, \mathrm{Pb^{2+}} raises it. Depressors at grain boundaries flatten the peak. Acceptors (Mn, Fe) pin walls; donors (La, Nb) make grains semiconducting.
  3. Grain size (below).
  4. Orientation and poling. A crystal has \kappa \approx 4000 normal to c but 400 along c; poling turns c axes towards the field and lowers \kappa along it.
  5. Internal stress from clamping by neighbouring grains or a substrate shifts the transitions.
  6. Field, frequency, time and porosity. A DC bias clamps walls and lowers \kappa; space charge adds below about 1 kHz; \kappa ages as walls are pinned; pores (\kappa = 1) dilute it.

Effect of grain size a (dense ceramics, 1 kHz):

  • a > 10 µm: \kappa(25^\circ\mathrm{C}) \approx 1500 to 2000 (plateau about 1700). 90° domains are about 0.8 µm wide whatever the grain size, and the Curie peak is sharp and tall.
  • 10 to 1 µm: a clamped grain balances wall energy against the elastic energy of its tetragonal misfit:
w_w = \frac{\sigma}{d}, \quad w_m = \frac{d\,c_{11}S_s^2}{128\pi a} \quad\Rightarrow\quad d = \sqrt{\frac{128\pi\sigma a}{c_{11}S_s^2}} \propto \sqrt{a}

With \sigma = 3\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-2}}, c_{11} = 1.7\times10^{11}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}, S_s = 0.01 this gives d \approx 0.8 µm at 10 µm. Finer grains hold more wall area per volume, \varepsilon_{r,\mathrm{dom}} \propto 1/d (\varepsilon_r \approx 1000 + 500/d, d in µm), so \kappa rises to a maximum of about 5000 at 0.8 to 1 µm.

  • a < 0.7 µm: tetragonality falls (c/a - 1 from 1.02% to below 1%), the lattice turns pseudocubic and 90° walls vanish below about 0.4 µm. \kappa drops (about 2400 at 0.28 µm) and the Curie peak broadens and smears out.

Walls also soften the ceramic (E = 168 GPa at 0.7 µm against 186 GPa at 0.3 µm). So dense, about 1 µm grains give the highest room-temperature \kappa, which is why capacitor bodies use grain-growth inhibitors.

7b.html:
Given: \Delta H = 2\ \mathrm{eV} per vacancy, T = 1000\ \mathrm{K}, u = 1.6 imes10^{-15}\ \mathrm{Hz} (normal atoms), u^{\prime} = 0.6 imes10^{-15}\ \mathrm{Hz} (atoms beside a vacancy), z = 4, 1\ \mathrm{eV} = 1.6 imes10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}, k = 1.38 imes10^{-23}\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}.

Find: the equilibrium vacancy fraction n/N and the number of vacancies.

Solution

Step 1, equilibrium condition. Forming n vacancies on N sites costs n(\Delta H - T\Delta S_v) and gains configurational entropy k\ln[N!/n!(N-n)!]. Setting \partial G/\partial n = 0 with Stirling's approximation and n \ll N:

rac{n}{N} = \exp\left( rac{\Delta S_v}{k} ight)\exp\left(- rac{\Delta H}{kT} ight)

Step 2, vibrational entropy (Einstein model). Each atom is three oscillators, each with entropy k[1 + \ln(kT/h u)] at high T. A vacancy softens the three oscillators of each of its z neighbours from u to u^{\prime}:

\Delta S_v = 3zk\ln rac{ u}{ u^{\prime}} \quad\Rightarrow\quad rac{n}{N} = \left( rac{ u}{ u^{\prime}} ight)^{3z}\exp\left(- rac{\Delta H}{kT} ight)

Step 3, numbers.

egin{aligned} rac{\Delta H}{kT} &= rac{2 imes 1.6 imes10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}}{(1.38 imes10^{-23}\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}})(1000\ \mathrm{K})} = 23.19, \qquad e^{-23.19} = 8.50 imes10^{-11} \ rac{\Delta S_v}{k} &= 3(4)\ln rac{1.6}{0.6} = 12 imes 0.981 = 11.77 \quad (\Delta S_v = 1.62 imes10^{-22}\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}) \ \left( rac{ u}{ u^{\prime}} ight)^{12} &= e^{11.77} = 1.29 imes10^{5} \ rac{n}{N} &= (1.29 imes10^{5})(8.50 imes10^{-11}) = 1.10 imes10^{-5} \end{aligned}

Step 4, number. Per mole of sites, n = (6.022 imes10^{23})(1.10 imes10^{-5}) = 6.6 imes10^{18}. With the slide's molar volume of MgO, 11.3\ \mathrm{cm^3\,mol^{-1}}, there are 5.33 imes10^{22} sites per \mathrm{cm^3}, so n = 5.9 imes10^{17}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}.

Answer: n/N \approx 1.1 imes10^{-5}, about 6.6 imes10^{18} vacancies per mole (5.9 imes10^{17}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}). The softer vibrations near a vacancy raise the count 1.3 imes10^{5} times above the bare Boltzmann value, 8.5 imes10^{-11}.
pts: States n/N = \exp(\Delta S_v/k)\exp(-\Delta H/kT) from minimising the free energy with configurational entropy
Vibrational entropy \Delta S_v = 3zk\ln( u/ u^{\prime}), so the pre-factor is ( u/ u^{\prime})^{3z}
Correct exponent \Delta H/kT = 23.19 and \exp(-23.19) = 8.5\times10^{-11}, with eV converted to J
Correct entropy factor: \Delta S_v/k = 11.77, (1.6/0.6)^{12} = 1.29\times10^{5}
Final vacancy fraction n/N \approx 1.1\times10^{-5}
Converts to a number: 6.6\times10^{18} per mole of sites or about 6\times10^{17}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}
Notes that only the ratio \nu/\nu^{\prime} matters (the printed 10^{-15} Hz does not enter)

8a(i).html:
\mathrm{Mg^{2+}} replaces \mathrm{Al^{3+}} in corundum, so each Mg on an Al site carries an effective charge of -1, \mathrm{Mg_{Al}^{\prime}}. \mathrm{Al_2O_3} has 2 cation sites for every 3 anion sites, and the compensating defect must keep that ratio.

Oxygen-vacancy compensation (the usual model):

2\mathrm{MgO} \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{Al_2O_3}\ } 2\mathrm{Mg_{Al}^{\prime}} + 2\mathrm{O_O^{\times}} + \mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}

Mass: 2 Mg and 2 O on each side. Sites: 2 Al sites to 3 O sites (two filled, one empty). Charge: 2(-1) + 2 = 0.

Alternatives that also balance:

3\mathrm{MgO} \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{Al_2O_3}\ } 2\mathrm{Mg_{Al}^{\prime}} + \mathrm{Mg_i^{\bullet\bullet}} + 3\mathrm{O_O^{\times}}
2\mathrm{MgO} + \tfrac12\mathrm{O_2(g)} \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{Al_2O_3}\ } 2\mathrm{Mg_{Al}^{\prime}} + 3\mathrm{O_O^{\times}} + 2h^{\bullet}\quad(\text{high } p_{\mathrm{O_2}})

For the vacancy route, electroneutrality gives [\mathrm{Mg_{Al}^{\prime}}] = 2[\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}], so [\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}] = (K a_{\mathrm{MgO}}^2/4)^{1/3}. This small MgO addition is the classic sintering aid for dense, translucent alumina.
pts: Writes Mg on an Al site as \mathrm{Mg_{Al}^{\prime}} (effective charge -1)

8a(ii).html:
Rock-salt BaO has only one cation site, so both \mathrm{Bi^{3+}} and \mathrm{Fe^{3+}} sit on \mathrm{Ba^{2+}} sites, each with an effective charge of +1: \mathrm{Bi_{Ba}^{\bullet}} and \mathrm{Fe_{Ba}^{\bullet}}. \mathrm{BiFeO_3} brings 2 cations but 3 oxygens, while BaO needs one cation site per oxygen site, so the third cation site is left empty.

Cation-vacancy compensation (expected in an oxidising atmosphere):

\mathrm{BiFeO_3} \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{BaO}\ } \mathrm{Bi_{Ba}^{\bullet}} + \mathrm{Fe_{Ba}^{\bullet}} + \mathrm{V_{Ba}^{\prime\prime}} + 3\mathrm{O_O^{\times}}

Mass: 1 Bi, 1 Fe, 3 O on each side. Sites: 3 Ba sites to 3 O sites. Charge: (+1) + (+1) + (-2) = 0.

Electronic compensation (reducing atmosphere), donor doping:

\mathrm{BiFeO_3} \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{BaO}\ } \mathrm{Bi_{Ba}^{\bullet}} + \mathrm{Fe_{Ba}^{\bullet}} + 2\mathrm{O_O^{\times}} + \tfrac12\mathrm{O_2(g)} + 2e^{\prime}

Sites 2:2, three O on each side, charge +2 - 2 = 0; this route makes BaO n-type.

For the vacancy route, electroneutrality is [\mathrm{Bi_{Ba}^{\bullet}}] + [\mathrm{Fe_{Ba}^{\bullet}}] = 2[\mathrm{V_{Ba}^{\prime\prime}}], and with [\mathrm{Bi_{Ba}^{\bullet}}] = [\mathrm{Fe_{Ba}^{\bullet}}] all three defects are equal, (K a_{\mathrm{BiFeO_3}})^{1/3}.

8b.fix: Slide 22 attributes the "magnetic locking" that keeps the train stable and centred to the Meissner effect. Complete flux expulsion only repels; it gives no restoring force sideways. Locking comes from flux pinning: in a type II superconductor between H_{c1} and H_{c2}, flux vortices are held by defects, so the superconductor resists any change of position relative to the magnet. In the coil-type train that slide 22 itself describes, neither effect acts: the centring comes from the cross-connected (null-flux) guideway coils.
8b.html:
Meissner effect. Below T_c (and below the critical field) a superconductor expels magnetic flux from its interior (slides 3, 5):

B = \mu_0(H + M) = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad M = -H, \qquad \chi = -1

It is a perfect diamagnet. Lossless screening currents in a surface layer about 0.1 \mum thick (the penetration depth) set up a field equal and opposite to the applied one, as if a mirror-image magnet with like pole faced the real magnet.

Why this levitates. The expelled field lines are squeezed between the magnet and the superconductor, and the compressed field pushes on the surface with a magnetic pressure

p = \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}

For B = 0.5 T, p \approx 99.5 kPa, enough to hold about 10 t per \mathrm{m^2}. The magnet rises until this repulsion equals its weight. In a type II ceramic such as YBCO, some flux enters as pinned vortices, which lock the gap and stop sideways drift.

Maglev train.

  • HTS maglev: YBCO blocks in liquid-nitrogen cryostats under the car, over a permanent-magnet track: flux expulsion and pinning lift and centre the car with no power, even at rest.
  • Superconducting maglev (Japan): persistent-current coils on the train induce currents in guideway coils as it moves; their opposing field (the same mirror principle in a normal metal) lifts the train about 10 cm. A linear motor propels it.

Conclusion: the assertion holds for a superconductor levitating over magnets; in the coil-type train, zero resistance makes the strong magnets and induction does the lifting.
pts: Meissner effect: flux expelled below T_c, B = 0 inside, perfect diamagnet \chi = -1
Lossless screening currents in a thin surface layer create an opposing (mirror-image) field
Levitation force from the compressed field, magnetic pressure B^2/2\mu_0, balancing the weight
Flux pinning in type II (YBCO) gives stable locking of the gap
Maglev example: superconductor on the train (YBCO over a magnet track, or SC coils inducing guideway currents), gap about 10 cm, linear-motor propulsion

• A perfect conductor would only freeze the flux it had; a superconductor expels flux even when cooled in the field. That expulsion, not zero resistance alone, defines the Meissner effect.

8c.html:
BCS theory (slides 7-10). An electron near the Fermi level distorts the positive-ion lattice; a second electron of opposite momentum and spin is drawn into the distortion. This phonon-mediated attraction binds them into a Cooper pair. All pairs share one coherent state, so scattering cannot stop the current, and breaking a pair costs an energy gap (meV):

2\Delta(0) \approx 3.52\,k_BT_c, \qquad T_c \approx 1.13\,\Theta_D\,e^{-1/N(0)V}, \qquad M^{\alpha}T_c = \text{const},\ \alpha = 0.5

Slide 11's mercury isotopes (4.185 K at 199.5 u, 4.146 K at 203.4 u) give \alpha \approx 0.48. BCS fits metals and alloys (Hg 4.15 K, Nb 9.2 K, \mathrm{Nb_3Sn} 18 K).

Cuprates (YBCO 92 K, Hg-Ba-Ca-Cu-O 133 K) break its assumptions:

Conclusion. Cooper pairs still exist (YBCO shows the flux quantum h/2e), but they are not bound by phonons. Strong electron correlation and antiferromagnetic spin fluctuations are the leading candidates; no theory is yet accepted.
